subject: Analytic form of joint distribution of two correlations in LKJ matrix

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Analytic form of joint distribution of two correlations in LKJ matrix
parts:
Hello all,

I have been trying to work out an analytic form for the joint density of two correlations in the LKJ matrix (e.g. rho(12) and rho(23)). From the Lewandowski et al. (2009) paper, I think I'm right (please correct me if I am wrong) in saying that the marginal distribution of a given correlation is given by a Beta(eta - 1 + d/2, eta -1 + d/2) - where d is the order of the matrix, and eta is a shape parameter - but I can't seem to find if there is an analytic form for the joint of two correlations.

Does anyone know if a joint distribution for two correlations exists, and if so, can you point me in its direction?

Best,

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Analytic form of joint distribution of two correlations in LKJ matrix
parts:
On Monday, August 10, 2015 at 6:19:47 PM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
Does anyone know if a joint distribution for two correlations exists, and if so, can you point me in its direction?

It depends on which two correlations you are referring to. Any two in the first column / row of the correlation matrix are independent, so the bivariate density is just the product of the marginal Beta densities over the (-1,1) interval. And each correlation in the second column / row depends on two correlations in the first column / row, so deriving a bivariate distribution would be difficult. It gets worse from there.

Ben

On Monday, August 10, 2015 at 8:59:18 PM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
Sorry for not being clear. Analytic expressions for the joint density of rho(23) with for example rho(34)? Alternatively, is there a paper on the uniform distribution over correlation matrices that you would recommend?

There is the LKJ paper, but that doesn't necessarily help. In general, it is true that if the Omega_{ij} is the partial correlation between variables i < j conditional on all variables prior to i and Sigma_{ij} is the usual Pearson correlation between i and j, then



So, according to the second line

Sigma_{23} = Omega_{12} * Omega_{13} +
                     Omega_{23} * sqrt( (1 - Omega_{12}^2) * (1 - Omega_{13}^2) )

and according to the third line

Sigma_{34} = Omega_{13} * Omega_{14} +
                     Omega_{23} * Omega_{24} * sqrt( (1 - Omega_{13}^2) * (1 - Omega_{14}^2) ) +
                     Omega_{34} * sqrt( (1 - Omega_{13}^2) * (1 - Omega_{14}^2) * (1 - Omega_{23}^2) * (1 - Omega_{24}^2) )

Although the Omegas are independently distributed and have a symmetric beta distribution on the (-1,1) interval with shape alpha_i = eta + (K - i) / 2, it is not easy to figure out the bivariate distribution of Sigma_{23} and Sigma_{34}, even if eta = 1 and K is large. There has to be a copula representation of their dependence, but I don't know what it is. And I'm not sure what the relevance to Stan would be. You could describe / plot it pretty well just by drawing the whole correlation matrix repeatedly from an LKJ distribution.

Ben
